new_statements.quote: 5.1.3.2 Druckakzent. Tucker/Bryan und Tucker sprechen in allen Arbeiten zum Kalenjin von 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' usw.; der Druckakzent scheint aber nach ihren Angaben mit Hochton oder Steigton korreliert zu sein, und markiert werden bei ihnen nur die Tonhöhen. [...] Bei meinen Aufzeichnungen habe ich keine Anzeichen für Druckakzent in phonemischer Funktion feststellen können und bezeichne ihn deshalb nicht. Phonetisch sind betonte Silben erkennbar, und zwar immer in Verbindung mit nicht-tiefem Ton.
new_statements.translation: 5.1.3.2 Stress accent. Tucker/Bryan and Tucker speak in all their works on Kalenjin of 'stressed syllables', 'shift in stress' etc.; but according to their data the stress accent appears to be correlated with high or rising tone, and they mark only the pitches. [...] In my own recordings I could find no evidence of stress accent in phonemic function and therefore do not mark it. Phonetically, stressed syllables are recognisable, always in combination with non-low tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalenjin (Rottland's description covers Terik as dialect unit 10, Elgon branch) is tonal (three tonemes); there is no contrastive/phonemic word stress; phonetic prominence is perceptible but not independently placed -- it always falls on a syllable bearing non-low (high or falling) tone. Terik-specific first-hand corroboration of the tonal system: Creider 1981: 29 (sec. 3.3) -- Terik preserves a three-way tonal contrast (H, L, HF); Creider says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kalenjin proper; Rottland notes that in Heine's (1973) Sogoo (Okiek) vocabulary stress is marked independently of tone and is 'not further predictable' there -- not applicable to Terik.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is pan-Kalenjin (based on Rottland's own field recordings of all 14 dialect units, Terik = no. 10); word-level phonetic prominence, not phrase-level; no Terik-specific stress statement exists in anything opened. The held text is a verbatim reconstruction from overlapping Google Books snippets (volumes 0ocOAAAAYAAJ/uzwaAQAAIAAJ), not a page scan.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Rottland 1982: 78) is pan-Kalenjin, made for all 14 dialect units of his own recordings; Terik [teri1244] is unit 10 (Elgon-Zweig: 6 Sapiny, 7 Kony, 8 Bong'om, 9 Pok, 10 Terik -- own Google Books snippet receipt plus the Anthropos 1984 review). The Terik-specific first-hand prosodic description (Creider 1981: 29, sec. 3.3) covers tone only. Sibling audits (tuge1241, okie1245, keiy1238) rest on the same Rottland paragraph. Do not confuse with Tetun-Terik (Austronesian, tetu1245), which dominates full-text search hits for 'Terik' + 'stress'.

sources.citation: Creider, Chet A. 1981. The tonal system of Proto-Kalenjin. In Thilo C. Schadeberg & M. Lionel Bender (eds.), Nilo-Saharan: Proceedings of the First Nilo-Saharan Linguistics Colloquium, Leiden, September 8-10, 1980, 19-39. Dordrecht: Foris.
sources.note: First-hand fieldwork (1979-80) on every Kalenjin dialect incl. Terik. Sec. 3.3 'TERIK' p. 29: Terik 'preserve[s] the earlier three-way tonal contrast' (H, L, HF), borrowed High Fall Lowering from Nandi, High Spreading restricted to primary suffixes. Purely tonal description; the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the chapter.
